blocks.label: Historical rates
blocks.alt: Overnight, one-month, three-month and six-month rates rise from near zero in 2022 to above 5% in 2023, then fall toward 3.5% to 4% by 2026.

blocks.text: A long period of lower rates gave way to high inflation and one of the fastest Fed hiking cycles in 2022.
The curve moved from yield pickup to path risk.
From a cash perspective, every decision starts with the same choice.
Stay short and keep the overnight rate or extend into term and lock a return for the period ahead.

items.text: Make cash work harder over the period.
Price the future before it happens.
The overnight rate represents the rate at which cash resets daily and moves closely with the Fed’s policy rate.
The gap between overnight and term reflects expected rate moves, risk premium and liquidity for the period.
Term rates look ahead. OIS, SOFR futures and Term SOFR are built differently, but they broadly reflect the market’s expected path for overnight rates over the period ahead.

blocks.text: Overnight tells us what cash earns today. Term rates put a price on that uncertainty.
A higher starting spread can look attractive, but realized return depends on what the Fed does next.

blocks.label: Priced premium vs. realized outcome
blocks.alt: Time series in basis points. The priced premium swings widely while realized excess returns fluctuate closer to zero.

blocks.text: The premium is visible at the start. The result is only known later.

sections.heading: Outcomes depend on the Fed path

blocks.text: The initial spread helps frame the trade-off, but it does not determine the result.
Daily decisions – choose the term and compare the results.

blocks.alt: Scatter plot of the initial six-month minus overnight spread against realized six-month excess return, both in basis points. Outcomes fall on either side of zero at a range of initial spreads.

blocks.text: The starting spread does not guarantee the excess return.

items.text: Locking the six-month rate beat rolling overnight over the same period.
Rolling overnight beat locking the six-month rate over the same period.

blocks.text: The initial term premium wasn’t enough. Overnight returns beat the term rate over the period.
Replay the same cycle upside down and term can switch from drag to protection.

blocks.text: When the path turns lower, locking term can switch from drag to protection.

items.text: Unexpected hikes or delayed cuts can erode the benefit of locking in.
Results improve when the market underprices future easing.

blocks.text: How should cash be allocated when the path is uncertain?

sections.heading: No single tenor wins in every scenario

blocks.text: Sticky paths reward term. Fast easing rewards liquidity. A diversified ladder lowers the cost of being wrong.

blocks.label: The scenarios · Rate paths over 36 months
blocks.alt: Five rate paths: renewed inflation, higher for longer, gradual normalization, faster normalization, and recession with rapid cuts.

blocks.label: The outcomes · Regret by scenario
blocks.alt: Horizontal bars compare regret in basis points for a term ladder, all overnight, and all six-month under five rate scenarios.

blocks.label: The alternatives · Simplified frontier
blocks.alt: The term ladder has the lowest worst-case regret of the three portfolios. All six-month has the lowest average regret.

blocks.text: 50% stays inside 3M for flexibility. 50% locks 6M carry.
Lower regret = lower cost of being wrong.
Set the objective — understand the trade-off.
Liquidity, yield and resilience compete for the same allocation. More of one usually means accepting less of another.

items.text: More term increases earnings certainty, but reduces flexibility if rates or liquidity needs change.
More short-term exposure increases flexibility, but leaves more return exposed to future rates.

items.term: Resilience · Reduce dependence on one rate path
items.text: A broader allocation can lower the cost of being wrong, but may give up some upside if one tenor proves best.

blocks.text: Build the model — capture what matters.

The model has the same trade-off: too simple can miss the risk; too complex can add assumptions, variables and noise. Add complexity where it materially improves the answer and supports the decision with confidence.
